quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on beam geometry, packing density and what the beam worksheet is telling you.

questions.q: In the beam formula, what do D, d and L stand for?
options: Loom width, reed width and warp length
Diameter of beam with yarn, barrel diameter and length between flanges
Flange diameter, yarn diameter and loom length
Beam density, yarn density and length of yarn
questions.explain: D is the full diameter of the yarn-covered beam, d the empty barrel and L the distance between the flanges; the yarn occupies the annulus between d and D along L.

questions.q: The yarn on a full beam is described geometrically as:
options: A hollow cylinder (a cylinder with the barrel removed)
questions.explain: The barrel occupies the centre, so the yarn volume is the full cylinder π/4 × D² × L minus the barrel π/4 × d² × L.

questions.q: Packing density in the lecture is expressed as:
questions.explain: The lecture gives about 56 in³ per lb for a warped beam and 60 in³ per lb for a sized beam, so weight = volume ÷ density.

questions.q: A sized beam has a higher packing density figure (60 in³/lb) than a warper's beam (56 in³/lb) because the size film makes the yarn bulkier.
questions.explain: Sized yarn carries a size film and winds less tightly, so each pound takes up more space: 60 in³ against 56 in³ for unsized yarn.

questions.q: Which quantity does the same beam carry LESS of once the yarn is sized, according to the worksheet?
questions.explain: The geometry (volume 50,385 in³) is unchanged, but at 60 in³/lb the sized beam holds 839.7 lb against 899.7 lb unsized.

questions.q: Why does the same beam hold 23,700 yd as a warper's beam but only 3,700 yd as a sized beam?
options: Sized yarn is six times heavier
The sized beam carries all 3,820 ends instead of 637, so the yarn length is shared among six times as many ends
The sized beam is wound at a lower density
The sizing machine cuts the warp into shorter lengths
questions.explain: Length = weight × 840 × Ne ÷ ends. With roughly six times the ends on the beam, each end's share of the yarn is about one sixth, giving one sixth of the yardage.

questions.q: 'Fabric from one sized beam' is less than the length of yarn on the beam because:
options: Some yarn is lost as waste at the knotting
The warp contracts in weaving, so the fabric is shorter than the warp
The beam must be left partly full
The weft takes up part of the length
questions.explain: At 10 % warp contraction, 3,693 yd of warp becomes 3,693 ÷ 1.1 = 3,357 yd of fabric.

questions.q: The length of yarn on a beam is found by dividing the weight by the count.
questions.explain: Length (yd) = weight × 840 × Ne ÷ ends on the beam. Ne multiplies, because a higher count means more yards per pound; and the result must be shared over the ends.

questions.q: The worksheet converts fabric per beam from yards to metres by:
questions.explain: A yard is 0.9144 m, so 3,357 yd × 0.9144 = 3,070 m. Multiplying by 1.0936 is the metres-to-yards direction.

questions.q: The lecture concludes that the 20,000 m order of Lecture 6 needs about how many sized beams?
questions.explain: 20,000 m ÷ 3,070 m per beam = 6.5, so 7 weaver's beams must be prepared; 6 would leave about 1,580 m unwoven.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The volume, weight and length formulas for a beam and how each input changes the answer.

questions.q: Yarn volume on a beam is:
questions.explain: The annulus area is π/4 × D² − π/4 × d² = π/4 × (D² − d²); (D − d)² is a common mistake and gives far too small a volume. π/4 × D² × L ignores the barrel.

questions.q: Weight of yarn on a beam (lb) equals:
questions.explain: Density is given as cubic inches per pound, so pounds = cubic inches ÷ (cubic inches per pound).

questions.q: Length of yarn on a beam in yards is:
questions.explain: weight × 840 × Ne is the total yards of yarn on the beam; dividing by the number of ends gives the length each end runs, which is the beam length.

questions.q: Doubling the length between flanges doubles the weight of yarn the beam can hold.
questions.explain: Volume is proportional to L, and weight is volume ÷ density, so twice the flange spacing holds twice the yarn (with the same D and d).

questions.q: If the outer diameter D is increased from 36" to 40" with d = 18" unchanged, the yarn volume rises by about:
questions.explain: Volume goes with D² − d²: 40² − 18² = 1,276 against 36² − 18² = 972; 1,276 ÷ 972 = 1.31, about 31 %. An 11 % rise in diameter gives more than 11 % in volume because of the square.

questions.q: With the same weight on the beam, putting twice as many ends on it:
questions.explain: Length = weight × 840 × Ne ÷ ends; the same total yardage is shared among twice as many ends, so each end (and the beam) is half as long.

questions.q: For a given beam and number of ends, changing from Ne 20 to Ne 40 yarn makes the length on the beam:
options: The same, because the volume is fixed
questions.explain: The beam holds the same weight, and Ne 40 has twice the yards per pound, so the length doubles (assuming the same packing density).

questions.q: Fabric from one sized beam equals:
questions.explain: The warp is longer than the cloth it makes by the contraction, so fabric = warp length ÷ 1.1 at 10 % contraction: 3,693 ÷ 1.1 = 3,357 yd.

questions.q: Because the sized beam has a higher in³/lb figure, it holds more pounds of yarn than the warper's beam of the same size.
questions.explain: More cubic inches per pound means fewer pounds in the same volume: 50,385 ÷ 60 = 839.7 lb against 50,385 ÷ 56 = 899.7 lb.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT change the number of sized beams needed for an order?
questions.explain: The beam count depends on fabric per beam, which comes from the beam volume, density, warp count, ends and contraction. The weft is not on the beam at all.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Volume, weight, yardage and fabric per beam, worked for the lecture's beam and for a larger one.

questions.q: A beam has D = 36", d = 18" and L = 66". What is the volume of the full cylinder, π/4 × D² × L, in cubic inches (to the nearest 10)?
For the same beam (d = 18", L = 66"), what is the volume of the barrel in cubic inches (to the nearest 10)?
questions.explain: π/4 × 18² × 66 = 0.7854 × 324 × 66 = 16,795 in³, one quarter of the full cylinder because 18 is half of 36.

questions.q: The yarn volume on a beam is 50,385 in³ and the packing density is 56 in³ per lb. What weight of yarn is on the beam, in lb (to one decimal)?
The same 50,385 in³ of yarn is sized, packing at 60 in³ per lb. What is the weight on the sized beam, in lb (to one decimal)?
questions.explain: Weight = 50,385 ÷ 60 = 839.75 ≈ 839.8 lb, about 60 lb less than the unsized beam.

questions.q: A warper's beam carries 899.7 lb of Ne 20 yarn on 636.67 ends (average). What length of yarn is on the beam, in yards (to the nearest 10)?
A sized beam carries 839.7 lb of Ne 20 yarn on 3,820 ends. What is the length of warp on the beam, in yards (to the nearest yard)?
A sized beam holds 3,693 yd of warp and the warp contraction is 10 %. How many metres of fabric will the beam weave (to the nearest 10 m)?
A larger beam has D = 40", d = 20" and L = 72". Find the yarn volume π/4 × (D² − d²) × L in cubic inches (to the nearest 10).
The 67,858 in³ of yarn on the larger beam is unsized (56 in³/lb). Its weight is closest to:
questions.explain: 67,858 ÷ 56 = 1,212 lb. 1,131 lb would be the sized figure (÷ 60) and 900 lb is the lecture's smaller beam.

questions.q: An order of 20,000 m is to be woven from sized beams that each give 3,070 m of fabric. How many beams are needed?
questions.explain: 20,000 ÷ 3,070 = 6.51, so 7 beams; a beam cannot be half prepared and 6 would leave the order short.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Loom-shed and sizing-room decisions that turn on how much yarn and fabric a beam holds.

questions.q: A weaving manager needs to know how many beam changes a 20,000 m order of fabric A will cause on the loom. Which worksheet figure answers this?
options: Length of yarn on the warper's beam
questions.explain: Fabric per sized beam (3,070 m) divided into the order length gives the number of beams and therefore beam changes: 20,000 ÷ 3,070 → 7 beams, 6 changes after the first.

questions.q: The sizing room wants fewer beam changes on the loom for a long order. Which change gives the most fabric per beam?
options: A beam with a larger barrel diameter d
A beam with a larger outer diameter D and longer L
Winding the warp at a looser density
Adding more size to the yarn
questions.explain: More fabric needs more yarn on the beam, which comes from a bigger annulus (larger D, longer L). A larger barrel removes volume, looser winding and more size both raise the in³/lb figure and reduce the pounds held.

questions.q: A mill buys beams with a 20" barrel instead of 18" for the same 36" outer diameter and 66" length. The yarn capacity:
options: Rises, because the barrel is stronger
Is unchanged, because D is the same
questions.explain: D² − d² changes from 1,296 − 324 = 972 to 1,296 − 400 = 896; 896 ÷ 972 = 0.92, a loss of about 8 % of the yarn volume.

questions.q: A planner uses the warper's beam packing density (56 in³/lb) for a sized beam. The sized beam weight will be:
options: Correct, because the volume is the same
questions.explain: 50,385 ÷ 56 = 899.7 lb instead of the true 839.7 lb at 60 in³/lb: 899.7 ÷ 839.7 = 1.07, about 7 % too high, and the fabric per beam would be overestimated by the same amount.

questions.q: If a loom shed weaves a 20,000 m order on 7 sized beams, the last beam will be only about half used.
questions.explain: Six full beams give 6 × 3,070 = 18,420 m, so the seventh beam supplies the remaining 1,580 m, about half of its 3,070 m.

questions.q: A merchandiser is asked how many metres of grey fabric A one weaver's beam yields for a sampling run. The quickest correct answer from the worksheet is:
questions.explain: 3,070 m is the fabric per sized beam. 3,357 is in yards, 3,693 yd is the warp length before contraction, and 23,700 yd is the warper's beam, not the weaver's.

questions.q: A warper's beam of 637 ends holds about 23,741 yd. Lecture 6 found that a 20,000 m order needs 24,059 yd of warp. What should the planner conclude?
options: One warper's beam set is just enough
The warp must be split, since one beam set holds slightly less than the order needs
The warper must run at a higher speed
questions.explain: 24,059 yd is about 1.3 % more than one beam can hold, so the set of 6 warper's beams cannot carry the whole order in one length; either two sets or a slightly shorter first set are needed.

questions.q: Which beam would weave the most fabric: (i) 36" D, 18" d, 66" L with Ne 20 at 3,820 ends, or (ii) the same beam with Ne 30 at 3,820 ends?
options: Cannot be told without the weft count
questions.explain: Both hold about 839.7 lb, but Ne 30 has 1.5 times the yards per pound, so beam (ii) carries about 5,540 yd and weaves about 1.5 times as much fabric.

questions.q: A loom is 72" wide but the beam between flanges is only 66". Which quantity in the beam calculation is directly limited by the 66"?
options: The number of ends on the beam
The length L in the volume formula
questions.explain: L is the length between flanges, 66" here. The ends on the beam are set by the fabric width and EPI, not by L.

questions.q: The sizing room reports that sized beams are coming out at 950 lb instead of the expected 840 lb for the same beam dimensions. The most likely explanation is:
options: The yarn count is finer than planned
The beam is wound harder (lower in³/lb) or carries much more size
questions.explain: Same volume but more weight means fewer cubic inches per pound: a harder wind, or a much heavier size add-on, puts more mass into the same space. Finer count or fewer ends would not raise the weight.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions linking beam geometry, count, ends and order planning across the whole lecture.

questions.q: A beam has D = 30", d = 18" and L = 66". It is wound unsized at 56 in³ per lb. What weight of yarn does it hold, in lb (to the nearest lb)?
The larger beam of the worked quiz holds 67,858 in³ of sized yarn at 60 in³/lb on 4,800 ends of Ne 30. What length of warp is on it, in yards (to the nearest 10)?
A student calculates the yarn volume as π/4 × (36 − 18)² × 66 = 16,795 in³. The mistake is:
options: Squaring the difference of the diameters instead of taking the difference of the squares
questions.explain: (D − d)² = 324 but D² − d² = 972; the correct annulus volume is three times larger, 50,385 in³.

questions.q: If the warp count, ends and beam dimensions are fixed, a sized beam always weaves less fabric than the same beam would hold as warp before sizing.
questions.explain: Two effects work the same way: sized yarn packs at 60 instead of 56 in³/lb, so fewer pounds fit, and warp contraction then shortens the fabric below the warp length.

questions.q: The lecture's sized beam weaves 3,070 m of fabric A. An order is for 35,000 m. How many sized beams must be prepared?
questions.explain: 35,000 ÷ 3,070 = 11.4, so 12 beams are needed; 11 would weave only 33,770 m.

questions.q: Two beams have the same volume. Beam P has 2,000 ends of Ne 20; beam Q has 4,000 ends of Ne 40. Which carries the longer warp?
questions.explain: Length = weight × 840 × Ne ÷ ends. Q has twice the Ne and twice the ends, so the two effects cancel and the lengths are equal at the same packing density.

questions.q: A beam calculation gives 3,357 yd of fabric but the planner needs the answer in metres and multiplies by 1.0936, reporting 3,671 m. The true figure is:
questions.explain: Yards to metres is × 0.9144: 3,357 × 0.9144 = 3,070 m. Using 1.0936 inflates the figure by about 20 % relative to the right answer.

questions.q: A sized beam carries 839.7 lb of Ne 20 on 3,820 ends. If the warp contraction is 12 % instead of 10 %, how many yards of fabric does the beam weave (to the nearest yard)?
questions.explain: Warp length = 3,693 yd; ÷ 1.12 = 3,297 yd, about 60 yd less than at 10 % contraction.

questions.q: The weight of a full warper's beam and an empty one are measured as 1,150 lb and 250 lb. The yarn is Ne 20 on 637 ends. The length of warp is about:
questions.explain: Yarn weight = 1,150 − 250 = 900 lb; × 16,800 = 15,120,000 yd; ÷ 637 = 23,736 ≈ 23,700 yd. Using the gross weight of 1,150 lb would give the wrong 30,300 yd.

questions.q: To weave 20,000 m of fabric A on exactly 6 sized beams instead of 7, which single change would be sufficient?
options: Increase the beam diameter D from 36" to about 38"
Increase the barrel diameter d from 18" to 20"
Reduce the number of ends per beam
questions.explain: Six beams need 3,333 m each, 8.6 % more than 3,070 m. Volume goes with D² − d²: 38² − 18² = 1,120 against 972, a 15 % gain, which is enough. A bigger barrel or more size holds less yarn, and fewer ends would change the fabric.
